lessonTitle: Annealing, Quenching and Tempering of Steel

blocks.text: A blacksmith plunges a red-hot chisel into water and it becomes glass-hard but shatters if dropped; reheated gently until its surface turns pale straw (about 230 degrees C), the same steel now holds an edge and survives a hammer blow. Heat treatment changes the microstructure, and so the properties, of one steel without changing its composition.

blocks.markdown: A steel's properties depend on its microstructure, which depends on how fast it is cooled from the austenite region. Slow cooling gives equilibrium products (ferrite and pearlite). Very fast cooling gives non-equilibrium martensite. Reheating martensite gives *tempered martensite*. Every heat treatment follows the same three steps: heat, hold and cool.

blocks.title: Martensite
blocks.text: A supersaturated body-centred tetragonal solid solution of carbon in iron formed from austenite by a diffusionless, shear-type transformation during rapid cooling. Its hardness depends mainly on carbon content, and it is hard and brittle.

rows: Austenitise (about 30 to 50 degrees C above the upper critical temperature)
Moderate strength and hardness, uniform grain
Very hard, brittle, high residual stress
Reheat quenched steel below 727 degrees C
blocks.caption: Typical steel heat treatments.

blocks.markdown: **Why quenching gives martensite.** To transform from austenite (FCC) to ferrite (BCC) plus cementite, carbon atoms must diffuse over distances of micrometres. If the steel is cooled faster than the *critical cooling rate*, this diffusion cannot happen. The iron lattice then changes by a coordinated shear, with no carbon redistribution, trapping carbon in the new lattice. This distorts it from cubic to body-centred tetragonal. Martensite is also dense in dislocations, so slip is very difficult and the steel is hard and brittle.

blocks.title: Will a quenched part become martensite?
blocks.prompt: A thin steel part cools from 800 degrees C to 500 degrees C in 1.2 s at the surface and in 6.0 s at the centre during a water quench. The steel's critical cooling rate over this range is 100 degrees C/s (assumed). Check each location.

steps.text: Calculate the average rate at the surface: $\Delta T/\Delta t$.
Compare with the critical rate of 100 degrees C/s: the surface exceeds it, the centre does not.

blocks.answer: The surface becomes martensite but the centre cools too slowly and forms pearlite or bainite, so the part is hard at the surface and softer at the core.

blocks.markdown: **Tempering.** As-quenched martensite is too brittle for use and has high residual stress. Reheating below 727 degrees C lets carbon diffuse out of the martensite to form fine carbide particles in a ferrite matrix (*tempered martensite*). The higher the tempering temperature, or the longer the time, the more the carbides grow and coarsen, the lower the strength and hardness, and the higher the ductility and toughness.

blocks.caption: Illustrative values for a medium-carbon (about 0.4 wt% C) steel. Actual values depend on composition and section size.

blocks.title: Choosing a tempering temperature
blocks.prompt: Using the illustrative table above, find the tempering temperature that gives about 42 HRC, assuming hardness varies linearly between 400 and 500 degrees C.

steps.text: Hardness falls from 45 HRC at 400 degrees C to 38 HRC at 500 degrees C: 7 HRC per 100 degrees C.
To go from 45 down to 42 HRC requires a 3 HRC drop.

blocks.answer: Temper at about 440 degrees C to reach roughly 42 HRC.

items: Quench cracking and distortion come from thermal gradients and the volume increase when martensite forms; use the mildest quenchant that exceeds the critical cooling rate.
Quench then temper is the standard route to a high-strength, tough steel; as-quenched is rarely used.
Low tempering (about 150 to 250 degrees C) retains hardness for tools and bearings; high tempering (about 500 to 650 degrees C) gives toughness for shafts and bolts.
Some steels lose toughness when tempered in an intermediate range (tempered martensite embrittlement), which is avoided in practice.

blocks.title: Select by target
blocks.text: Choose the process by working backward from the target: maximum softness or machinability, anneal; uniform moderate properties, normalise; maximum hardness, quench and low temper; a given hardness with toughness, quench and temper at the interpolated temperature.

points: Cooling faster than the critical rate suppresses carbon diffusion and gives hard, brittle martensite.
Tempering reheats martensite below 727 degrees C, precipitating carbides; higher tempering temperatures lower hardness and raise toughness.
Heat treatments are selected by target: anneal to soften, normalise for uniformity, quench and temper to reach a stated hardness and toughness.

questions.stem: Martensite forms in a steel when austenite is cooled faster than the critical cooling rate. What kind of transformation is this?

options.text: A diffusionless (shear) transformation in which carbon stays trapped in solution
A diffusional transformation producing alternating plates of ferrite and cementite
A eutectic reaction from the liquid
A recrystallisation of ferrite grains

questions.correctOptionText: A diffusionless (shear) transformation in which carbon stays trapped in solution

distractorRationale.a: Correct: no long-range diffusion occurs, so the carbon stays in the lattice.
distractorRationale.b: This describes pearlite, which forms on slow cooling.
distractorRationale.c: Martensite forms from solid austenite, not from the liquid.
distractorRationale.d: Recrystallisation is a restoration process in cold-worked metal, not a phase transformation of austenite.

questions.explanation: When cooling is very fast, carbon atoms have no time to diffuse out of the FCC austenite lattice to form cementite. The lattice then shears into a body-centred tetragonal structure with the carbon trapped, which is martensite.

questions.stem: Why does rapid quenching of a medium-carbon steel from the austenite region give a very hard but brittle structure?

options.text: Carbon cannot diffuse out, so it is trapped in a supersaturated, distorted body-centred tetragonal lattice that strongly resists dislocation motion
Quenching melts the steel and refines the grains
Quenching removes carbon from the steel surface
Quenching forms large equiaxed ferrite grains

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon cannot diffuse out, so it is trapped in a supersaturated, distorted body-centred tetragonal lattice that strongly resists dislocation motion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the trapped carbon distorts the lattice and martensite also has a high dislocation density.
distractorRationale.b: Quenching occurs wholly in the solid state; nothing melts.
distractorRationale.c: Carbon is not removed; it is retained in solid solution.
distractorRationale.d: Large ferrite grains would be soft; quenching prevents their formation.

questions.explanation: Because carbon is retained in solution, the transformed lattice is highly strained, and martensite is also full of dislocations and fine twins. These features block dislocation motion, giving high strength and hardness but little ductility.

questions.stem: Raising the tempering temperature of a quenched medium-carbon steel generally decreases its hardness and increases its toughness.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Higher tempering temperatures allow more carbon to leave the martensite and form carbides, and the matrix recovers, so strength and hardness fall while ductility and toughness rise. This is the basis of choosing the tempering temperature to balance the two.

questions.stem: A thin section is quenched from 800 degrees C and passes through 500 degrees C after 2.5 s. Calculate the average cooling rate over this range in degrees C per second. (For comparison, assume the steel needs at least 80 degrees C/s to avoid pearlite formation.)
questions.explanation: The average cooling rate is $\Delta T/\Delta t=(800-500)/2.5=120$ degrees C/s. Because this exceeds the assumed critical rate of 80 degrees C/s, the austenite will transform to martensite rather than pearlite.

questions.stem: For a particular quenched steel the hardness after tempering was measured as 48 HRC at 350 degrees C and 34 HRC at 550 degrees C (assumed data). Assuming hardness varies linearly with tempering temperature between these points, calculate the tempering temperature needed to give 40 HRC, in degrees C.
questions.explanation: Linear interpolation: hardness falls 14 HRC over 200 degrees C, i.e. 0.07 HRC per degree C. To drop from 48 to 40 HRC needs 8 HRC, so $\Delta T=8/0.07=114.3$ degrees C and $T=350+114.3=464.3$ degrees C. The linear assumption is an approximation of a smooth curve.

questions.stem: A shaft made from a 0.40 wt% C steel must have a good balance of strength and toughness (hardness around 30 to 40 HRC). Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.text: Austenitise, quench in oil or water, then temper at about 450 to 600 degrees C
Austenitise and quench only, leaving it as quenched
Full anneal by slow furnace cooling
Quench and temper at 150 degrees C for maximum hardness

questions.correctOptionText: Austenitise, quench in oil or water, then temper at about 450 to 600 degrees C

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tempering in this range gives the target hardness with good toughness.
distractorRationale.b: The as-quenched martensite would be too hard and brittle, with high internal stresses.
distractorRationale.c: Full annealing gives soft coarse pearlite and ferrite, below the target strength.
distractorRationale.d: A low temper retains most of the martensitic hardness and has lower toughness than needed.

questions.explanation: The target hardness is well below the as-quenched hardness (about 55 HRC or more for 0.4 wt% C), so a tempering temperature in the 450 to 600 degrees C range is used to trade excess hardness for toughness. Quenching first creates martensite, which tempering then turns into fine carbides in ferrite.

questions.stem: Rank these quenchants by the severity of cooling for a given part, from the fastest to the slowest cooling rate.

options.text: Water, then oil, then still air
Oil, then water, then still air
Still air, then oil, then water
Water, then still air, then oil

questions.correctOptionText: Water, then oil, then still air

distractorRationale.a: Correct: water extracts heat fastest, oil is intermediate and still air is slowest.
distractorRationale.b: Water has higher cooling severity than oil; this order is reversed at the start.
distractorRationale.c: This is the reverse of the correct ranking.
distractorRationale.d: Still air is slower than oil; this misplaces air.

questions.explanation: Water has a high heat-extraction rate, especially in the vapour-blanket breakdown stage, so it gives the fastest quench. Oil cools more gently, with lower risk of distortion and cracking, and still air is slowest, as in normalising.

questions.stem: What happens to the microstructure of martensite when it is tempered at, say, 500 degrees C?

options.text: Carbon precipitates as fine cementite particles in a ferrite matrix, relieving the lattice strain
It reverts to austenite
It becomes coarse pearlite
It becomes liquid

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon precipitates as fine cementite particles in a ferrite matrix, relieving the lattice strain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the structure is called tempered martensite.
distractorRationale.b: Tempering temperatures lie well below the eutectoid temperature of 727 degrees C, so austenite does not re-form.
distractorRationale.c: Pearlite forms by cooling austenite, not by tempering martensite at this temperature.
distractorRationale.d: 500 degrees C is far below the melting point of steel.

questions.explanation: At tempering temperatures carbon diffuses out of the supersaturated martensite and forms fine carbides, and the lattice relaxes from body-centred tetragonal toward body-centred cubic. This tempered martensite is much tougher, but somewhat softer.

questions.stem: Explain why a 0.45 wt% C steel furnace-cooled slowly from the austenite region is soft with ferrite and pearlite, whereas the same steel quenched in water from the same temperature is very hard. Refer to carbon diffusion and the resulting crystal structures.
markingGuide: Slow cooling allows carbon to diffuse, so austenite decomposes into ferrite and cementite (pearlite) (2 marks)
The structure is made of soft ferrite and lamellar pearlite with low hardness (1 mark)
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion; austenite transforms by shear without carbon redistribution (2 marks)
Carbon remains trapped in a distorted body-centred tetragonal lattice (martensite) (1 mark)
Martensite is hard because of lattice strain, high dislocation density and fine structure (2 marks)
Mentions that cooling must exceed the critical cooling rate (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The two treatments differ in whether carbon has time to diffuse. Slow cooling gives equilibrium products (ferrite and pearlite), while rapid quenching traps the carbon and produces the highly strained martensite.

questions.stem: A 0.40 wt% C steel crankshaft journal must have a final hardness between 35 and 40 HRC with the best toughness available at that hardness. The following illustrative tempering data apply: as-quenched 55 HRC; tempered at 400 degrees C, 45 HRC; at 500 degrees C, 38 HRC; at 600 degrees C, 31 HRC. Propose a complete heat treatment, including approximate tempering temperature, and justify each step. State what you assume about interpolation.
markingGuide: Austenitise above the upper critical temperature (about 830 to 860 degrees C) and soak to dissolve carbide and give uniform austenite (1 mark)
Quench at a rate above the critical rate (oil or water) to form martensite (1 mark)
Do not leave as-quenched: too hard and brittle with residual stress (1 mark)
Temper: 40 HRC at about $400+100\times(45-40)/7=471$ degrees C and 35 HRC at about $500+100\times3/7=543$ degrees C, so temper in the 470 to 540 degrees C range (3 marks)
Choose the upper end for more toughness, the lower end for more hardness (1 mark)
Assumes linear interpolation between data points and that part size does not alter results (1 mark)
Note possible tempered-martensite embrittlement for some steels in an intermediate range (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The crankshaft journal needs martensite first, so it is austenitised and quenched. Tempering in the range implied by the data, roughly 470 to 540 degrees C, then brings the hardness to 35 to 40 HRC, with tougher tempered martensite than the as-quenched state.
